body.objective: Students will be able to play concert scales.
successCriteria: I can play the concert B♭, E♭ and F major scales
I can explain how a major scale is built
I can play scales with good tone and even rhythm
body.hook: Professional musicians warm up with scales every day. It's not just tradition: scales train your fingers, your ears and your sense of key all at once. Most of the music your band plays is built from these patterns.

vocabulary.definition: A series of notes moving step by step from one note to the same note an octave higher or lower.
A scale with the pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half.
A distance of two half steps on the keyboard.
The smallest distance between two notes in Western music.
The pitch as it sounds on a piano; many band instruments read different notes for the same sound.
The distance from one note to the next note with the same name.

study.title: Scale Builders
study.question: How are scales built, and why do musicians practise them?
study.passage:
The major scale pattern: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half (W W H W W W H).
Concert B♭ major: B♭ C D E♭ F G A B♭
Concert E♭ major: E♭ F G A♭ B♭ C D E♭
Concert F major: F G A B♭ C D E F
Transposing instruments: When the band plays concert B♭, B♭ instruments (clarinet, trumpet, tenor saxophone, baritone treble clef) read C major; E♭ instruments (alto and baritone saxophone) read G major; French horn in F reads F major; flute, oboe, trombone, euphonium, tuba and mallets read B♭ major. Check your scale sheet.
Part 1, Build (10 minutes): On a keyboard diagram, mark whole and half steps and build concert B♭ major using W W H W W W H.
Part 2, Play (15 minutes): Play each scale in whole notes, then half notes, then quarter notes at a metronome setting of 72. Focus on steady air and matching tone across the band.
Part 3, Scale games (10 minutes): "Echo": the teacher plays a pattern from the scale, the band echoes. "Scale in thirds": play 1-3, 2-4, 3-5 and so on.
Part 4, Self-check: record yourself on one scale and listen for even rhythm, tone and correct notes.

body.objective: Students will be able to use legato and staccato articulation.
body.iCan: I can use legato and staccato articulation.
successCriteria: I can play legato and staccato articulations clearly
I can choose articulation to fit the style
body.hook: Say "too-too-too" and then "doo-doo-doo." Hear the difference? Wind players use their tongue in different ways to make notes smooth and connected or short and bouncy. That's articulation.

vocabulary.definition: How notes are started, connected or separated.
Smooth and connected, often with a soft "doo" tongue.
Short and separated, shown by a dot above or below the note.
A curved line over different notes: tongue only the first note.
A note played with extra emphasis, shown by >.
A line over a note meaning hold it for its full value.

study.title: Smooth or Short
study.question: How do articulations change the sound?
study.passage:
Articulation guide (written for this lesson; percussion uses sticking and stroke height for the same effects):
Normal tongue: "too": clear start, full length.
Legato tongue: "doo": gentle start, notes connected.
Staccato (dot): "tut": short, but the air still moves; the gap comes from shortening, not from choking the sound.
Slur (curve over different notes): tongue only the first note; change fingerings with steady air.
Accent (>): stronger air at the start, then back to normal.
Tenuto (–): full value, slight weight.
Activities: 1. Play Concert B♭ C D E♭ F with each articulation at 80 BPM. 2. Slur in pairs: slur 2, tongue 2. 3. Slur all five up and down. 4. Partner listening: play one articulation; partner names it. 5. Style: play "Hot Cross Buns" legato (sweet), then staccato (bouncy). Which suits a march?

body.objective: Students will be able to expand my range.
successCriteria: I can extend my range up and down using lip slurs or register exercises
I can keep a good tone across my range
I can use healthy habits that prevent strain
body.hook: Professional players can play from the lowest notes on their instrument to the highest with a steady, full tone. Range grows slowly, through daily habits, not by forcing high notes.

vocabulary.definition: The span from the lowest to the highest note a player can play well.
A part of an instrument's range, such as low, middle or high.
A brass exercise moving between notes on the same valve combination using air and lips.
A higher note in the natural series above a fundamental.
A key on clarinet or saxophone (octave key) that moves notes to a higher register.
The ability to play for a long time without tiring.

study.title: Stretching Your Range
study.question: How do musicians expand their range safely?
study.passage:
Range routines (written for this lesson; teachers adjust for each instrument):
Brass: lip slurs on open (0) valves: Concert B♭ to F to B♭ (trumpet written C–G–C). Use faster air and slight lip firmness to go up; don't press the mouthpiece harder. Rest as much as you play.
Flute: harmonics: finger low notes and blow faster, focused air to get the octave above; keep lips relaxed.
Clarinet: practise crossing the "break" between low and high registers; keep right-hand fingers down where possible.
Saxophone: octave-key slurs: low to middle register with steady air.
Percussion: extend mallet range on keyboard percussion; practise smooth movement across the whole instrument.
All: add one new note above or below each week; play long tones on it at mf; stop if you feel pain.
Track: write your lowest and highest comfortable note today, and set a goal for four weeks.
